subject: ent
title: Chronic otitis media and cholesteatoma

steps.tx: Chronic otitis media means persistent middle ear with mastoid inflammation, drum **perforation** and discharge lasting weeks. Safe tubotympanic disease shows a central perforation with mucosal infection and conductive loss but low complication risk. Unsafe atticoantral disease shows attic or marginal perforation harbouring **cholesteatoma** that erodes toward brain, labyrinth and facial nerve. Duration with perforation separates chronic disease from **recurrent acute** episodes.
steps.say: Chronic ear disease is perforation with discharge that is kept returning. Central holes are markers of safer mucosal disease with conductive loss. Attic or marginal holes are warnings of cholesteatoma with erosion risk. Duration beyond weeks separates chronic disease from recurrent acute infections. Brain, labyrinth and facial nerve are all within reach of unsafe disease.

steps.tx: Cholesteatoma means keratinising squamous epithelium growing where it should not, trapping desquamated **keratin** that expands, infects with Pseudomonas and anaerobes, and erodes ossicles, labyrinth and tegmen. Acquired disease follows **retraction pockets** from Eustachian dysfunction sucking the attic inward, or migration through marginal perforations. Congenital **cholesteatoma** grows behind an intact drum in children without prior infection.
steps.say: Cholesteatoma is skin in the wrong place with destructive power that is feared. Trapped keratin is expanding, infecting and eroding bone toward balance and brain. Retraction pockets from poor ventilation are the cause of most acquired cases. Marginal perforations provide another route inward. Congenital cases grow behind an intact drum in children.

vis.alt: Diagram showing acquired cholesteatoma formation. A retraction pocket in the tympanic membrane's attic invaginates, accumulating keratin debris that expands and erodes ossicles.
vis.caption: Cholesteatoma: acquired formation via retraction pocket or migration. Image: welleschik, CC BY 2.5, Wikimedia Commons.

steps.tx: Patients report painless foul **discharge** unresponsive to drops, conductive deafness, and sometimes vertigo, facial weakness or headache warning of complications. Otoscopy shows attic crust or white **keratin mass**, audiometry grades conductive against sensorineural loss, CT of the temporal bone maps **erosion**, and diffusion MRI detects residual pearls after surgery. Foul painless discharge that ignores drops should always raise cholesteatoma suspicion.
steps.say: Foul painless discharge that ignores drops points toward cholesteatoma. Conductive deafness with an attic crust or white mass is highly suspicious. Vertigo, facial weakness or headache is a warning of complications beyond the middle ear. Temporal bone scanning maps erosion before surgery while diffusion imaging finds residual disease. Audiometry grades the hearing loss precisely.

steps.tx: This endoscopic view shows an attic **retraction pocket** filled with white keratin debris plus adjacent ossicular **erosion** with discharge. The pocket marks acquired cholesteatoma formation where the attic invaginates and traps skin. Link the white mass to painless foul discharge, conductive loss, and CT mapped erosion toward **surgical clearance** rather than drops alone.
steps.say: This close view is a reminder of cholesteatoma in memory. The attic is a display of a retraction pocket packed with white keratin debris. Adjacent erosion with discharge is a marker of bone destruction in progress. The picture explains painless foul discharge with conductive loss. Scans map the extent before surgery because drops never remove trapped skin.

vis.alt: Endoscopic close-up of tympanic membrane showing attic retraction pocket filled with white keratin debris and adjacent ossicular erosion with discharge.
vis.caption: Otoscopic view of retraction pocket with keratin debris and ossicular erosion. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Treatment is surgical because drops only temporise infected discharge. **Mastoidectomy** removes disease and creates a safe dry ear, with tympanoplasty reconstructing drum and ossicles where possible. Canal wall up surgery preserves anatomy but risks hidden **recurrence** needing second look, while canal wall down surgery exteriorises disease for surveillance at the cost of a **mastoid cavity** needing lifelong care.
steps.say: Mastoidectomy is the clearance of disease while tympanoplasty is the rebuilding of hearing where possible. Canal wall preservation keeps normal anatomy but risks hidden recurrence. Canal wall removal improves surveillance at the cost of lifelong cavity care. Drops alone are never a cure for the underlying skin growth.

right.title: Unsafe CSOM
points: Bone erosion, brain and labyrinth risk

steps.tx: Safe central perforations stay dry with **water precautions**, receive aural toilet with topical therapy for flares, and gain **myringoplasty** once dry to improve hearing and infection resistance. Children with bilateral disease and deafness need hearing support meanwhile. Any chronic ear with vertigo, palsy or fever turns **urgent**, because labyrinthitis, facial involvement and intracranial spread move fast.
steps.say: Safe perforations need dry ears, clean flares and planned closure. Water precautions with aural toilet and topical therapy control discharge. Myringoplasty once dry improves hearing and resistance. Children with bilateral disease are given hearing support during waiting. Vertigo, facial weakness or fever with chronic ear disease is urgent and needs same day review.
